source: Muldoon and Weisberg (2011) Robustness and idealization in models of cognitive labor
finding: Tested the Kitcher (1990) and Strevens (2003) priority-rule models by weakening two idealizations. The models were not robust. Under some weakenings they predicted the opposite of the original result.
numbers: No numbers seen. Abstract-level only, via search snippets.
limits: Full text not opened (PDF blocked). Only the abstract-level claim is recorded. Exact weakened assumptions not verified here.
agent_relevance: Do not trust a payoff-based allocation rule just because one model says it spreads effort well. Test any S3 allocation rule under weakened assumptions.

source: Weisberg and Muldoon (2009) Epistemic Landscapes and the Division of Cognitive Labor
finding: Agent model on a landscape of research approaches. Mavericks avoid visited approaches. Followers move to approaches that proved fruitful. Authors claimed mixed populations are ideal.
numbers: Per Thoma's reading (b04, b05): 400 Mavericks find >90% of significant approaches within 200 periods; 400 Followers stagnate at 17%.
limits: Original paper not opened. Numbers come from Thoma's secondary description, which I did read.
agent_relevance: Pure following of past success stalls. A rule that steers agents away from already-visited approaches finds far more.

source: Fernandez Pinto and Fernandez Pinto (2018) Epistemic Landscapes Reloaded
finding: Re-implemented the Weisberg-Muldoon landscape model in a second language (FreePascal). The original code logic was correct. Small changes to agent rules changed results a lot.
numbers: No numbers seen. Catalog abstract only.
limits: Full paper (Historical Social Research 43(1)) blocked, not opened. Robust to implementation, not across the parameter space.
agent_relevance: Result of allocation sims is sensitive to agent rules. Keep the S3 rule simple and measure it on our own tasks.

source: Thoma (2015) The Epistemic Division of Labor Revisited
finding: Re-ran the Weisberg-Muldoon idea. Showed that in the original model homogeneous Mavericks beat every mixed group, so the claim that mixes are ideal is not supported by their own data.
numbers: Original model: 400 Mavericks find >90% of significant approaches in 200 periods. 400 Followers reach only 17%. About 1,000 approaches found by Followers in 500 periods, roughly 3 per agent.
quote: Mixed populations of Followers and Mavericks do not outperform homogeneous Mavericks by their own measures
limits: Secondary reading of the 2009 paper. Cost of Mavericks was only argued informally by the original authors.
agent_relevance: A mix of explorers and exploiters is not automatically better. Check whether the pure explorer arm wins before adding a split.

source: Thoma (2015) The Epistemic Division of Labor Revisited
finding: Thoma's own NetLogo model (Explorers vs Extractors, 50 repetitions per setting). Diversity of strategy helps only if agents can move medium or long range. With local movement it does not help.
numbers: Local movement, groups of 40: after 50 rounds pure Explorers had found 15% of significance, 50/50 mix 8%. Mix wins by a tiny margin after 300 rounds, when 90% is found already. Medium range (range 10): mix beats both pure groups, p<0.0001, two-sample t tests.
quote: diversity of research strategy is not beneficial when real world scientists are too uninformed and short-sighted
limits: Toy 2-D landscape with two hills. Range of movement was only run up to 10 for compute reasons.
agent_relevance: A division of labour only pays if exploiters can see and adopt what explorers find. In our agent, the code must put the explorers' finds in front of the exploiting step.

source: Thoma (2015) The Epistemic Division of Labor Revisited
finding: Mixed groups also cut variance. A mix reduced the spread of outcomes, which lowers risk for the community.
numbers: After 150 steps at medium range: standard deviation 12.5 percentage points for pure Extractors vs 3.1 for a mix with 40% Explorers.
limits: Same toy model, single parameter regime.
agent_relevance: A small share of forced explorers is a variance cut as well as a mean gain. Useful argument for reserving a fixed fraction of S3 budget.

source: Thoma (2015) The Epistemic Division of Labor Revisited
finding: With global movement, diversity still helps but progress is slower than at medium range, because the lower of two hills is neglected once the higher is found.
numbers: Qualitative: described in section 4.3, no exact figures read for this case.
limits: Authors argue medium range is the realistic case. Explorer rule was adapted for compute reasons (pilot runs showed no significant difference).
agent_relevance: Total freedom to switch can starve the weaker direction. Allocation code should guarantee a minimum share per untried direction.

source: Wu (2024) Better than Best: Epistemic Landscapes and Diversity of Practice in Science
finding: Agents on NK landscapes (N=20) that copy a randomly chosen better neighbour end with higher final scores than agents that copy the best neighbour. The best-copy group converges faster but gets stuck.
numbers: Two communities of 100 agents each, 1000 simulations per setting, N=20 (over a million solutions). Better-beats-best held in more than 74% of all parameter combinations and 100% when social learning happens less often than every round (V>1).
limits: Fails when social learning is every round. Toy binary NK model. Not an empirical test.
agent_relevance: Always copying the current best direction collapses diversity. Choose a random better option sometimes, not always the top one.

source: Wu (2024) Better than Best: Epistemic Landscapes and Diversity of Practice in Science
finding: The better-than-best advantage grows with connectivity. Best-copy accuracy drops significantly as the network gets more connected, while the better-copy community stays accurate.
numbers: Figure 3 setting N=20, K=5, V=5. Exact values only in figures, not read.
limits: Replicates earlier Lazer-Friedman and Zollman results on speed-accuracy trade-off in a new paradigm.
agent_relevance: If sub-agents see each other's results often (shared scratchpad), diversity dies. Delay sharing between explorers.

source: Wu (2024) Better than Best: Epistemic Landscapes and Diversity of Practice in Science
finding: Mixed communities: best-copiers free-ride on better-copiers. They gain early and still end well, but the better-copiers pay.
numbers: N=20, K=10, V=3, 40% better-copiers: mixed community scores above all-best and below all-better.
limits: Incentive problem is described, not solved.
agent_relevance: Free-riding is a design risk. If one arm of our agent is rewarded for the early best, the exploring arm needs a protected budget.

source: Kitcher (1990) The Division of Cognitive Labor; Strevens (2003) The Role of the Priority Rule in Science
finding: Founding models: the priority rule (credit to the first discoverer) pushes some scientists toward less promising projects, which spreads effort better than pure self-interest.
numbers: No numbers recorded. Described only via critics' summaries.
limits: Originals not opened. Muldoon and Weisberg (2011) report the result fails under weakened assumptions. Wu (2024) notes credit alone may attract people to under-staffed topics.
agent_relevance: Our agent has no credit system. The equivalent is code that pays an exploration bonus for under-sampled directions.

source: Zollman (2010) The Epistemic Benefit of Transient Diversity
finding: Cited by Wu (b07-b09): sparser communication networks keep more options alive for longer and learn more accurately but more slowly.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Only the secondary summary in Wu (2024) was read. Original not opened.
agent_relevance: Slow, partial sharing between parallel attempts is a lever, not a loss.

source: Choi et al. (2026) Do Multi-Agent LLMs Explore Each Other?
finding: LLM agents choosing between two peers lock onto one early and stay, even GPT-5. Selection counts are bimodal (near 0 or near 50 of 50 rounds), unlike UCB.
numbers: Two-armed delegation, pA=0.6, pB=0.5, T=50 rounds, 30 independent runs. Qwen2.5-7B, GPT-4, GPT-5 tested.
quote: LLM agents commit prematurely to one peer within the first few rounds
limits: Small bandit, arithmetic questions. NeurIPS 2026 workshop paper.
agent_relevance: A pure-prompt agent will not spread effort over approaches on its own. Allocation must be code, as the schema S3 says.

source: Choi et al. (2026) Do Multi-Agent LLMs Explore Each Other?
finding: Giving the UCB formula in the prompt only half fixes lock-in. An external calculator that supplies the scores removes it. The LLM can act on supplied exploration scores.
numbers: Qwen-7B, pA=0.6 vs pB=0.4. Inferior-peer lock-in: prompt-only 50.0%, with UCB formula 23.3%, with UCB calculator 0.0%, algorithmic UCB 0.0%. Cumulative regret 20.0, 13.5, 9.9, 9.8.
limits: One small model, one bandit instance. Multiple temperatures pooled in the paper.
agent_relevance: Strongest direct support for code-side allocation: code computes the scores, the model only picks or writes the attempt.

source: Choi et al. (2026) Do Multi-Agent LLMs Explore Each Other?
finding: MACE (contextual-bandit peer selection) spreads queries across peers. In-context exploration, prompted to balance explore and exploit, often does worse than random peer choice.
numbers: Seven models, four families, three benchmarks (HotpotQA, Math500, GPQA); 10 agents in the HotpotQA case. Exact accuracy tables in appendix, not summarized here.
quote: In-context exploration often underperforms even random peer selection
limits: Peer selection is not the same as picking research approaches. Regret bound needs a linear-bandit assumption.
agent_relevance: Prompting alone is an unreliable allocator. Random is a stronger baseline than a prompted explorer; test against random.

source: Choi et al. (2026) Do Multi-Agent LLMs Explore Each Other?
finding: Theory: a greedy selector has linear expected regret on a constructed stationary instance (premature commitment). MACE has order sqrt(T log T) regret.
numbers: Theorems 1-2 and Corollary 1; regret gap grows linearly in T.
limits: Constructed instance; assumes realizable linear rewards.
agent_relevance: Formal reason to reserve forced exploration, matching the Kitcher-style argument for spreading effort.

source: Krishnamurthy et al. (2024) Can Large Language Models Explore In-Context?
finding: GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Llama2 in multi-armed bandits did not explore robustly. Only one configuration worked: GPT-4 with chain-of-thought, a hint to explore, and externally summarized per-arm statistics.
numbers: GPT-4 basic prompt: suffix failure (best arm never chosen again after some round) in more than 60% of replicates. T=100 main runs, N=10 or 20 replicates; T=500 check with N=20. GPT-3.5: 48 prompt configurations, N=20.
quote: only one configuration resulted in satisfactory exploratory behavior
limits: Small replicate counts for GPT-4 (N=10, 10 configs). Simple bandits only. Models are older than 2026 models.
agent_relevance: Reliable exploration needed external summarization. Same lesson: let code keep the per-direction counts.

source: Krishnamurthy et al. (2024) Can Large Language Models Explore In-Context?
finding: A second failure mode: models pick all arms about equally and never narrow down. So both too little and too much spread occur.
numbers: Three GPT-4 configurations avoided suffix failures; two of them showed this uniform-like failure.
limits: Qualitative description of Figures 3-5.
agent_relevance: Allocation code needs both a floor (try every untried direction) and a stopping rule (drop losers).

source: Wang et al. (2024) Diversity of Thought Improves Reasoning Abilities of LLMs (DIV-SE)
finding: Asking the model for several different solution approaches, then running each, beats repeated sampling with the same prompt on hard planning and colouring tasks.
numbers: GPT-4: Blocksworld 3 zero-shot CoT 70%, self-consistency 10 samples 73%, DIV-SE 94%. Graph colouring: CoT 15%, SC-10 23%, IDIV-SE +59 points, DIV-SE 97%. Blocksworld 4/5: CoT 40%, SC-10 41.2%, gain 29.6 points. Reported AQUA-RAT gains up to 16.52 points (GPT-3.5).
quote: linguistic token diversity does not always ensure diverse and independent solution approaches
limits: Colouring used an external sound verifier to pick the answer. Benchmarks are narrow. Error propagation between in-call approaches estimated under 6.5%.
agent_relevance: Approach-level diversity beats sampling-level diversity. This is the closest LLM analogue of dividing labour by approach.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Diversity of Thought Improves Reasoning Abilities of LLMs (DIV-SE)
finding: Cost view: the approach-diverse method reached the same accuracy as sampling at lower cost.
numbers: Blocksworld 3: DIV-SE zero-shot beats SC-10 few-shot at 4 times lower cost, per the paper.
limits: Cost figures from the authors' own figure; not rechecked.
agent_relevance: Fewer, different attempts can be cheaper than many similar ones.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Mixture-of-Agents Enhances LLM Capabilities
finding: Layered mixes of different open models beat GPT-4o on AlpacaEval 2.0. Different models as proposers beat the same model sampled repeatedly at every proposer count.
numbers: AlpacaEval 2.0 LC win rate: MoA 65.1% vs GPT-4o 57.5%. Table 3, Qwen1.5-110B aggregator, 2 layers: n=6 multiple-proposer 61.3% vs single-proposer 56.7%; n=3 58.0 vs 56.1; n=2 58.8 vs 54.5.
limits: LLM-judge benchmark, win rate not accuracy. Gains partly come from more tokens and a strong aggregator.
agent_relevance: Heterogeneity helps proposers. For us one model is used, so diversity must come from prompts or assigned approaches.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Mixture-of-Agents
finding: Models differ in role: WizardLM is a good proposer but a poor aggregator, so division of labour by role matters.
numbers: Aggregator vs proposer scores (Table 4): WizardLM 8x22B 52.9% as aggregator vs 63.8% as proposer; LLaMA-3-70b 45.0% vs 60.6%; Qwen1.5-110B 61.3% vs 56.7%.
limits: Single benchmark, 2 layers.
agent_relevance: Separate the generate step from the pick step. Different skills.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
finding: Many independent attempts raise coverage a lot, but picking the right one without a verifier plateaus. Spread alone is not enough, a selector matters.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite with DeepSeek-Coder-V2: 15.9% with 1 sample, 56% with 250 samples (prior single-sample SOTA 43%). MATH, Llama-3-8B-Instruct: coverage 82.9% at 100 samples to 98.44% at 10,000; majority vote or reward model only 40.50% to 41.41%.
limits: Samples are independent draws of one model, not different approaches. 128 problems per math dataset.
agent_relevance: Allocation of effort needs a verifier or test to be worth it. Without one, extra spread is wasted.

source: Li et al. (2024) More Agents Is All You Need
finding: Plain sampling-and-voting performance grows with the number of agents, with larger gains on harder tasks.
numbers: Abstract-level only, no figures read.
limits: Only the abstract and intro were read. Voting among similar attempts; not approach-level division.
agent_relevance: Baseline to beat: a split-by-approach design must beat plain voting at equal budget.

source: Si, Yang and Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas?
finding: LLM idea generation saturates. Over-generating gives mostly duplicates, even when the prompt lists earlier ideas and asks to avoid repeating them.
numbers: Of 4000 generated seed ideas per topic, only about 200 (about 5%) were non-duplicates at cosine similarity 0.8 (all-MiniLM-L6-v2). The share of new non-duplicates per batch falls and total unique ideas plateau.
quote: out of the 4000 generated seed ideas, there are only 200 non-duplicate
limits: Embedding threshold of 0.8 chosen by manual inspection. NLP research ideas only.
agent_relevance: Asking the same model for more directions gives few new ones. Untried directions must be tracked and enforced by code, with duplicate checks.

source: Jiang et al. (2025) Artificial Hivemind: The Open-Ended Homogeneity of Language Models
finding: Different LLMs give similar answers to open-ended prompts, so using several models does not buy as much diversity as expected.
numbers: Infinity-Chat, 26K prompts, 42 models: within-prompt pairwise similarity averaged 0.821. Across models similarity ranges 71% to 82%; DeepSeek-V3 vs qwen-max 0.82. With min-p decoding, 81% of response pairs still above 0.7 and 61.2% above 0.8.
limits: Embedding similarity is a proxy for idea diversity. Open-ended chat prompts, not research tasks.
agent_relevance: Model heterogeneity and sampling temperature are weak diversity levers. Diversity should come from the assigned approach.

source: Liang et al. (2024) Encouraging Divergent Thinking in LLMs through Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Self-reflection suffers degeneration of thought: once confident the model will not produce new ideas. Debate between agents with opposed stances partly fixes this.
numbers: Counter-Intuitive Arithmetic (200 questions): GPT-3.5 26.0%, +CoT 28.0, +self-consistency 29.5, +self-reflect 27.5, +MAD 37.0; GPT-4 51.0.
quote: once the LLM has established confidence in its solutions, it is unable to generate novel thoughts later through reflection
limits: Small dataset. Debate adds cost. Gains over self-consistency modest (7.5 points).
agent_relevance: Same model alone does not diverge from its first answer. Forcing a different stance or approach is needed.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (MAST)
finding: Multi-agent LLM systems often fail, and failures come mostly from design and agent misalignment, not weak models.
numbers: 1600+ annotated traces, 7 frameworks; failure rates 41% to 86.7%; kappa 0.88; categories: system design 41.8%, inter-agent misalignment 36.9%, task verification 21.3%. ChatDev 86.7% failure, MetaGPT 60.0% on ProgramDev.
limits: Failure rate is on the authors' tasks, not a general rate. Not specific to approach allocation.
agent_relevance: Splitting work across agents has a real failure cost. Single-agent code-side allocation avoids inter-agent misalignment.

source: Gottweis et al. (2025) Towards an AI co-scientist
finding: A generate-debate-evolve system with a tournament of hypotheses improves ranked hypothesis quality as more compute is spent. Selection by pairwise ranking is what drives the gain.
numbers: 203 research goals; hypotheses split into ten time buckets; average Elo of top 10 and best Elo both rise across buckets.
limits: Elo is self-judged by the system's own ranker; the paper reports expert validation separately (not read here).
agent_relevance: Generate many, rank with a tournament. A spread-then-select loop works at scale, but ranker quality limits it.

source: Zhu et al. (2026) SYMPHONY: Synergistic Multi-agent Planning with Heterogeneous Language Model Assembly
finding: A pool of different LLMs expanding MCTS branches gives far more distinct branches than one model, and accuracy rises with branch diversity.
numbers: Share of expansions with 4 unique branches: above 80% for the three-model ensemble vs under 20% for a single model on MBPP. SYMPHONY-S (small open models): HotpotQA EM 0.59, WebShop 0.56 SR, MBPP 0.927; SYMPHONY-L: 0.79, 0.72 SR, 0.965 (Python). Branches 2/3/4: HotpotQA 0.34/0.47/0.59.
limits: Authors' own implementation; baselines taken from papers. Three runs averaged. Adversarial prompting and temperature scaling gave only marginal diversity (Appendix I).
agent_relevance: Prompt and temperature tricks add little diversity; assigning different generators does. Gains from more branches are steep up to 4 and not tested beyond.

source: Zhu et al. (2026) SYMPHONY
finding: Ablations: removing agent scheduling, memory sharing or the exploration-based MCTS step each cut accuracy a lot.
numbers: Ablation (SYMPHONY-S): HotpotQA 0.59 falls to 0.51 without agent scheduling, 0.45 without memory sharing, 0.51 without EMCS; WebShop 0.56 to 0.48/0.46/0.49; MBPP 0.927 to 0.906/0.871/0.892.
limits: Single study, three tasks, mean of 3 runs.
agent_relevance: Scheduling which generator takes which branch and sharing what was tried both matter, which is what an S3 allocation table does.
